name: Scar massage

lead: Scar massage means applying repeated pressure, stretching or circular movement to a healed scar to make it softer, flatter and more flexible, and to ease tightness and itch. Surgeons, burn units and physical therapists commonly recommend it.

Proposed mechanisms include mechanically remodelling collagen in the scar tissue. Wikipedia cites a 2012 review reporting weak evidence of benefit, mainly for surgical incision scars, and a 2022 scoping review of 25 studies that reported favourable outcomes with inconsistent methods.

paras: People massage the scar by hand, often with a lotion or oil, once the wound has closed, usually as a daily routine over weeks to months. Regimens vary greatly in timing, duration and technique.
Massage is generally regarded as low risk. Open or healing wounds are typically handled under clinical guidance.

angle.text: Pressing and stretching a healed scar by hand is used to soften the tissue and leave a flatter, more flexible scar that is less noticeable. Clinics commonly recommend it, and reviews describe the evidence as limited, with varied methods.

lead: Scar massage is the manual application of pressure, stretching or circular movement to a scar, typically after the wound has closed, to improve its texture, flexibility and appearance and to relieve symptoms such as tightness and itch [1][2].

It is widely used in burn units and surgical aftercare. A 2012 review in Dermatologic Surgery noted that many surgeons recommend postoperative massage but that regimens vary greatly [2], and a 2018 systematic review began by noting that massage is used in burn units globally while the supporting evidence was unknown [3].

Overall, published reviews describe the evidence as limited and heterogeneous. Wikipedia summarises a 2012 review as finding weak evidence of benefit, mainly for surgical incision scars, and a 2022 scoping review of 25 studies as reporting favourable outcomes but inconsistent methods and outcome measures [4].

paras: Scar massage covers a range of techniques, from circular rubbing with the fingers to deeper stretching or manipulation, sometimes with a lotion or oil to reduce friction. A review of regimens found they differed in time to onset, scar location, duration and technique [2].
Massage is often combined with other scar-management measures such as silicone products and pressure garments, which complicates assessment of its separate effect [1].

A 2016 literature review of high-level studies of scar-management methods, published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, noted that numerous scar products are marketed and that their efficacy is unclear [1].

Systematic reviews focused on burns report limited and variable results [3][5]. A 2022 scoping review of massage for post-operative scarring also examined this question [6]. Wikipedia reports that a 2012 review found weak evidence of benefit, mainly for surgical incisions, and that the 2022 scoping review of 25 studies found favourable outcomes but inconsistent methodology [4].

Human research includes the 2012 review of massage regimens [2], a 2018 systematic review of scar massage for hypertrophic burn scars [3], a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of massage on burn scars [5], and a 2022 scoping review on post-operative scars [6]. These reviews describe small studies with varied protocols and conclude that stronger trials are needed.
Scar massage appears in lifestyle-oriented appearance discussions as a low-cost, at-home scar-care practice. No community material on it is cited here.
